extracted.intended_audience: investors, stewardship teams, corporate boards, and governance professionals (proxy voting and engagement practitioners)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance used by an investor stewardship team (BIS/BlackRock) to assess corporate governance, executive pay, climate/natural capital disclosures, board composition and to determine voting and engagement actions at shareholder meetings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Director independence
rubrics_metrics.description: Director independence — from management, significant shareholders, or other related parties — is a central tenet of sound corporate governance across markets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look to boards to have a sufficient number of independent directors, free from conflicts of interest or undue influence, to ensure objectivity in board decision-making and oversight of management; generally consider it good practice for independent directors to make up a majority of the board, or in the case of controlled companies, at least one-third. Examples and case studies (First Pacific) illustrate how insufficient independence influences voting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Director tenure and disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: Local market norms treat director tenure as a factor affecting independence (e.g., Hong Kong capping INED tenure at nine years). BIS looks for disclosure to explain an independent classification when a director has nine or more years of service.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where companies consider long-serving directors independent, provide sufficient information explaining the classification; BIS may not consider long-tenured directors independent, and lack of disclosure can lead BIS to withhold support for re-election (First Pacific example). Tenure can also affect committee independence and overall board independence calculations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Board composition
rubrics_metrics.description: In assessing board composition, BIS takes into account a company’s board size, business model, strategy, market capitalization, ownership structure, and the market in which the company operates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Companies should explain how their approach to board composition supports governance practices and provide sufficient information on individual nominees so shareholders can assess capabilities, suitability, and fit within overall board composition (see CTBC Holding case).

rubrics_metrics.name: Director capacity / overcommitment
rubrics_metrics.description: Directors must be able to commit an appropriate amount of time to board and committee matters; excessive roles can impair a director’s ability to fulfill duties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Best practice is for directors not to take on an excessive number of roles; when concerns about overcommitment arise (e.g., serving on several listed company boards while holding an executive role), BIS may engage, communicate capacity-related concerns, and can withhold support until issues are addressed (Carlsberg example).

rubrics_metrics.name: Committee independence
rubrics_metrics.description: Board committees (e.g., nomination, audit, remuneration) should have appropriate independent membership.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If committees are not majority independent it may indicate insufficient oversight and can be a reason for BIS to withhold support for director elections or related proposals (First Pacific noted several committees were not majority independent).

rubrics_metrics.name: Board governance framework and role clarity
rubrics_metrics.description: Companies should establish and maintain a robust framework of effective governance mechanisms, including clear descriptions of the role of the board and the committees and how directors engage with and oversee management.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clear role descriptions and governance frameworks, alongside disclosure of material risks and oversight processes, support investors’ assessment of board effectiveness and alignment with long-term financial interests (Spotlight on AI oversight reference).

rubrics_metrics.name: Board oversight of generative and agentic AI
rubrics_metrics.description: When AI is material to a company’s business, companies should disclose how AI-related factors are assessed by management and overseen by the board.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good practice includes boards seeking to remain abreast of company-specific AI strategies and broader AI advancements, disclosing AI-related risk assessment and embedding AI governance into board and committee processes (HubSpot example). BIS engages with companies to understand AI oversight and may consider this in voting and engagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incentives aligned with financial value creation (executive compensation alignment)
rubrics_metrics.description: Executive compensation should be an important tool to support long-term financial value creation by rewarding delivery of strategic, operational, and/or financial goals, encouraging an appropriate risk appetite, and aligning shareholders and executives via equity ownership.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: BIS finds it helpful when companies clearly connect compensation policies and outcomes to long-term shareholder interests. BIS reviews rigor relative to company strategy and market context and may not support compensation-related proposals or responsible directors if compensation is misaligned with long-term financial performance (statistics on support and non-support provided).

rubrics_metrics.name: Compensation disclosure and linkage between pay and performance
rubrics_metrics.description: Companies should make clear in disclosures how compensation policies and outcomes link to the financial interests of long-term shareholders and to company performance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: BIS closely reviews disclosures to determine whether the board’s approach is rigorous and clearly articulated; insufficient disclosure or unclear linkage can lead to engagement and voting against compensation-related proposals or committee members (Shopify and Takeda examples).

rubrics_metrics.name: Design of incentive arrangements (balance, measures, vesting)
rubrics_metrics.description: When assessing pay, BIS considers the balance between fixed and variable pay, the selection of performance measures and associated targets, the length of vesting and/or holding periods, and the overall complexity of incentive arrangements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: BIS looks for transparent, cogent explanations of how executive pay supports strategy and incorporates long-term financial value drivers; length of vesting/holding periods and whether awards are time-based or performance-based are important (EMEA spotlight and Sage example).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of discretion and awards outside established plans
rubrics_metrics.description: Concerns include the use of discretion by remuneration committees, awards outside of established plans, limited linkage between pay outcomes and long-term financial performance, or insufficient explanation of program design.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such practices are common focus areas (noted particularly in the U.S. and Continental Europe); BIS may take case-by-case action including engagement and voting against related proposals or directors if explanations or controls are inadequate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integration of sustainability metrics into compensation
rubrics_metrics.description: Linking sustainability targets (e.g., GHG emissions reduction goals) to executive compensation is a practice companies use to align pay with sustainability performance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: BIS considers explicit integration of credible sustainability metrics (e.g., Linde tying 20% of a strategic non-financial award to GHG goals) as part of its assessment of whether remuneration supports long-term value creation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Climate-related risk disclosure and transition planning
rubrics_metrics.description: For companies facing material climate-related risks, BIS finds it helpful when they publicly disclose, consistent with their business model and sector, how they intend to deliver long-term financial performance through the low-carbon transition, including, where available, their transition plan.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: BIS uses disclosures and engagement to understand strategies, scenario analysis, board oversight and management actions; inadequate disclosure of climate oversight can lead BIS to withhold support for director elections or other proposals. While transition plans can be helpful, BIS does not make preparation of a transition plan a voting issue by itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Natural capital governance (land use/deforestation, water, biodiversity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Where natural capital is financially material, BIS focuses on governance of key components — land use and deforestation, water, and biodiversity — which may affect long-term financial returns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Companies should disclose how nature-related impacts and dependencies are managed and how boards oversee these risks. Robust governance and oversight of natural capital supports durable financial value creation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Water risk management
rubrics_metrics.description: Sectors heavily dependent on fresh water should assess and manage water-related risks given scarcity and potential regulatory restrictions in water-stressed locations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: BIS observes material performance differences between companies in areas experiencing water stress; companies operating in exposed sectors (agriculture, pharmaceuticals, manufacturing, apparel, food & beverage, tech) should disclose governance and management approaches to water risk.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessment of shareholder proposals’ scope and economic merit
rubrics_metrics.description: When evaluating shareholder proposals (particularly on climate/nature), BIS assesses whether proposals are over-reaching, lack economic merit, or seek outcomes unlikely to promote long-term financial value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: BIS often withholds support when proposals are redundant or address issues companies already have processes to manage; under BIS’ Benchmark Policies in 2025 the team did not support shareholder proposals on climate/nature when considered over-reaching or lacking economic merit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Voting responses to engagement findings
rubrics_metrics.description: BIS uses voting (against director elections, compensation proposals, board report approvals, or against shareholder proposals) as a lever when engagement or disclosure is inadequate or policies are misaligned with long-term shareholder interests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Voting outcomes depend on issues identified (independence, disclosure, misaligned pay, climate oversight, etc.). Examples and aggregate statistics illustrate when BIS supported or withheld support for management recommendations and directors across regions.
